ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Eligible participants were children, adolescents and young adults aged 1-34 years with cliniciandocumented type 1 diabetes.

> The participants had been in diabetes care for at least six months and were attending routine follow-up at one of the four participating clinics.

> Written informed consent was obtained from participants aged ≥18 years and from parents or guardians of minors, with age-appropriate assent obtained from children and adolescents where applicable.

> Participants were recruited consecutively during routine clinic visits at each study site.

> A total of 260 participants were enrolled: 92 from Kenyatta National Hospital, 72 from Machakos Level 5 Hospital, 51 from Westlands Level 4 Hospital, and 45 from Kajiado County Referral Hospital.

> Participants were classified as euthyroid when both TSH and FT4 were within the laboratory reference intervals.

> The paired TSH-FT4 matrix demonstrated that most participants were euthyroid (n=189).

> A notable finding was that 11.5% of participants had discordant TSH-FT4 profiles, most commonly normal TSH with either low or elevated FT4.

> Male participants had approximately twice the adjusted odds of hypothyroidism compared with females, although this did not reach statistical significance (aOR 2.13, 95% CI 0.87-5.20; p=0.098).

> Written informed consent was obtained from all participants aged 18 years and older.

> For participants younger than 18 years, written informed consent was obtained from a parent or legal guardian, with age-appropriate assent obtained from the child or adolescent before enrolment.

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethical approval was obtained from the Kenyatta National Hospital-University of Nairobi Ethics and Research Committee (P291/04/2026).

> All study procedures were conducted in accordance with applicable ethical standards and regulations.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.05", Text = "Odds ratios (ORs), adjusted odds ratios (aORs), 95% confidence intervals and two-sided p-values were reported, with statistical significance defined as p<0.05."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.073", "p=0.098", "p=0.100", "p=0.651", "p=0.098"), Sentence = c("The prevalence was higher among males than females (15.2% vs 7.5%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.073).", "Male sex was associated with approximately twofold higher adjusted odds of hypothyroidism, although this did not reach statistical significance (aOR 2.13, 95% CI 0.87-5.20; p=0.098).", "Age (aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.90-1.01; p=0.100) and duration of T1D (aOR 1.02, 95% CI 0.93-1.13; p=0.651) were also not statistically significant, figure 5.", "Age (aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.90-1.01; p=0.100) and duration of T1D (aOR 1.02, 95% CI 0.93-1.13; p=0.651) were also not statistically significant, figure 5.", "Male participants had approximately twice the adjusted odds of hypothyroidism compared with females, although this did not reach statistical significance (aOR 2.13, 95% CI 0.87-5.20; p=0.098)." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

live_data_statements: Eligible participants were children, adolescents and young adults aged 1-34 years with cliniciandocumented type 1 diabetes.
The participants had been in diabetes care for at least six months and were attending routine follow-up at one of the four participating clinics.
Written informed consent was obtained from participants aged ≥18 years and from parents or guardians of minors, with age-appropriate assent obtained from children and adolescents where applicable.
Participants were recruited consecutively during routine clinic visits at each study site.
A total of 260 participants were enrolled: 92 from Kenyatta National Hospital, 72 from Machakos Level 5 Hospital, 51 from Westlands Level 4 Hospital, and 45 from Kajiado County Referral Hospital.
Participants were classified as euthyroid when both TSH and FT4 were within the laboratory reference intervals.
The paired TSH-FT4 matrix demonstrated that most participants were euthyroid (n=189).
A notable finding was that 11.5% of participants had discordant TSH-FT4 profiles, most commonly normal TSH with either low or elevated FT4.
Male participants had approximately twice the adjusted odds of hypothyroidism compared with females, although this did not reach statistical significance (aOR 2.13, 95% CI 0.87-5.20; p=0.098).
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants aged 18 years and older.
For participants younger than 18 years, written informed consent was obtained from a parent or legal guardian, with age-appropriate assent obtained from the child or adolescent before enrolment.
